claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) is known to be a critical site for movement initiation and motor learning.
source: The primary motor cortex (M1) is known to be a critical site for movement initiation and motor learning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: M1 has been shown to possess reward-related activity, presumably to facilitate reward-based learning of new movements.
source: Surprisingly, it has also been shown to possess reward-related activity, presumably to facilitate reward-based learning of new movements.
evidence: This refers to prior work showing reward-related activity in M1, cited in the introduction.

claim: Most of the major neuronal cell types in M1 showed robust but differential responses to both the conditioned cue stimulus (CS) and reward.
source: Our results demonstrate that most of the major neuronal cell types in M1 showed robust but differential responses to both the conditioned cue stimulus (CS) and reward, and their response properties undergo cell-type-specific modifications after associative learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the imaging data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: Neuronal response properties in M1 undergo cell-type-specific modifications after associative learning.
source: Our results demonstrate that most of the major neuronal cell types in M1 showed robust but differential responses to both the conditioned cue stimulus (CS) and reward, and their response properties undergo cell-type-specific modifications after associative learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by longitudinal imaging data comparing days 1 and 7.

claim: PV-INs' responses became more reliable to the CS after associative learning.
source: PV-INs' responses became more reliable to the CS, while VIP-INs' responses became more reliable to reward.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing increased reliability of PV-IN responses to CS on day 7.

claim: VIP-INs' responses became more reliable to reward after associative learning.
source: PV-INs' responses became more reliable to the CS, while VIP-INs' responses became more reliable to reward.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing increased reliability of VIP-IN responses to reward on day 7.

claim: Pyramidal neurons only showed robust responses to novel reward.
source: Pyramidal neurons only showed robust responses to novel reward, and they habituated to it after associative learning.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E and Figure 6 showing PN responses to reward on day 1 but not day 7.

claim: Pyramidal neurons habituated to reward after associative learning.
source: Pyramidal neurons only showed robust responses to novel reward, and they habituated to it after associative learning.
evidence: This is supported by data showing decreased PN responses to reward on day 7 compared to day 1.

claim: SOM-INs' responses emerged and became more reliable to both the CS and reward after conditioning.
source: Lastly, SOM-INs' responses emerged and became more reliable to both the CS and reward after conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2H and 6 showing increased SOM-IN responses on day 7.

claim: Within M1, neurons encode movement goals and movement kinematics.
source: Within M1, neurons encode movement goals and movement kinematics (Georgopoulos et al., 1992; Moran and Schwartz, 1999; Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons in M1 have been reported to show reward-related activity in nonhuman primates.
source: In vivo recording studies performed in nonhuman primates found neurons in M1 that encode reward anticipation, reward delivery, and mismatches between the two (Marsh et al., 2015; Ramakrishnan et al., 2017; Ramkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in nonhuman primates.

claim: Reward has been shown to modulate M1 activity in human subjects, likely through an inhibitory circuit-dependent mechanism.
source: In human subjects, reward has also been shown to modulate M1 activity, likely through an inhibitory circuit-dependent mechanism (Thabit et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study in humans.

claim: In well-trained mice performing a skilled reaching task, a subset of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in M1 specifically report successful, but not failed, reach-and-grasp movements.
source: It was recently shown that in well-trained mice performing a skilled reaching task, a subset of layer 2/3 (L2/3) pyramidal neurons (PNs) in M1 specifically report successful, but not failed, reach-and-grasp movements.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levy et al., 2020.

claim: A different subset of PNs report only failed reach-and-grasp movements.
source: In contrast, a different subset of PNs report only failed reach-and-grasp movements (Levy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levy et al., 2020.

claim: Associative learning using reinforcement can accelerate and enhance learning.
source: It is widely accepted that associative learning using reinforcement can accelerate and enhance learning (Abe et al., 2011; Nikooyan and Ahmed, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Positive feedback (reward) facilitates motor memory retention.
source: In the case of motor learning, studies have demonstrated that positive feedback (reward) facilitates motor memory retention and negative feedback (punishment) speeds up the learning process (Galea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galea et al., 2015.

claim: Negative feedback (punishment) speeds up the learning process.
source: In the case of motor learning, studies have demonstrated that positive feedback (reward) facilitates motor memory retention and negative feedback (punishment) speeds up the learning process (Galea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galea et al., 2015.

claim: Different IN subtypes have been shown to have distinct gene expression profiles, electrophysiological properties, and connectivity motifs.
source: Different IN subtypes have been shown to have distinct gene expression profiles, electrophysiological properties, and connectivity motifs (Fishell and Rudy, 2011; Markram et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SOM-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PNs to filter synaptic inputs.
source: Some studies have demonstrated that SOM-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PNs to filter synaptic inputs, fast-spiking PV-INs preferentially target perisomatic regions of PNs enabling strong inhibition of spiking, and VIP-INs regulate local microcircuits by controlling other local INs (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Fast-spiking PV-INs preferentially target perisomatic regions of PNs enabling strong inhibition of spiking.
source: Some studies have demonstrated that SOM-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PNs to filter synaptic inputs, fast-spiking PV-INs preferentially target perisomatic regions of PNs enabling strong inhibition of spiking, and VIP-INs regulate local microcircuits by controlling other local INs (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: VIP-INs regulate local microcircuits by controlling other local INs.
source: Some studies have demonstrated that SOM-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PNs to filter synaptic inputs, fast-spiking PV-INs preferentially target perisomatic regions of PNs enabling strong inhibition of spiking, and VIP-INs regulate local microcircuits by controlling other local INs (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Visual orientation selectivity in PNs is modulated and sharpened by PV- and SOM-INs in the primary visual cortex.
source: Multiple studies using in vivo opto-recordings in the primary visual cortex have shown that visual orientation selectivity in PNs is modulated and sharpened by PV- and SOM-INs (Atallah et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PV- and SOM-INs exert control over PN frequency tuning in the primary auditory cortex.
source: In the primary auditory cortex, PV- and SOM-INs exert analogous control over PN frequency tuning (Seybold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seybold et al., 2015.

claim: In the auditory cortex, prefrontal cortex, and basolateral amygdala, reinforcement signals such as reward and punishment have been shown to recruit VIP-INs, which in turn, inhibit SOM- and PV-INs.
source: Moreover, in the auditory cortex, prefrontal cortex, and basolateral amygdala, reinforcement signals such as reward and punishment have been shown to recruit VIP-INs, which in turn, inhibit SOM- and PV-INs (Krabbe et al., 2019; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mice learned to associate the CS with the reward after 7 days, shown by an increase in anticipatory lick rate.
source: Mice learned to associate the CS with the reward after 7 days, shown by an increase in anticipatory lick rate, a conditioned response, following the cue onset on day 7 compared to day 1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C comparing lick rates on days 1 and 7.

claim: On day 1, the mean lick rate during ITI lick bouts (1.47 ± 0.17/s) and the CS (1.37 ± 0.17/s) were similar.
source: On day 1, the mean lick rate during ITI lick bouts (1.47 ± 0.17/s) and the CS (1.37 ± 0.17/s) were similar, while the lick rate following reward delivery was significantly higher (7.16 ± 0.48/s).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements presented in the results.

claim: On day 1, the lick rate following reward delivery was significantly higher (7.16 ± 0.48/s) than during ITI or CS.
source: On day 1, the mean lick rate during ITI lick bouts (1.47 ± 0.17/s) and the CS (1.37 ± 0.17/s) were similar, while the lick rate following reward delivery was significantly higher (7.16 ± 0.48/s).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: On day 7, the lick rate during the CS period (3.42 ± 0.37/s) was significantly higher than during ITI lick bouts (1.71 ± 0.2/s).
source: In contrast, on day 7 following associative learning, the lick rate during the CS period (3.42 ± 0.37/s) was significantly higher than during ITI lick bouts (1.71 ± 0.2/s), demonstrating that the mice effectively learned the CS–reward association by day 7 (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: All cell types showed a similar proportion of active cells (irrespective of the behavioral task) on days 1 and 7.
source: We compared the mean percentage of active cells within the entire session to ensure all cell types had a similar proportion of active cells (irrespective of the behavioral task) on days 1 and 7 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PV-IN and VIP-IN cell types had a percent of CS- and reward-responsive cells that were significantly greater than chance level on both days 1 and 7.
source: Surprisingly, we found that only PV-IN and VIP-IN cell types had a percent of CS- and reward-responsive cells that were significantly greater than chance level on both days 1 and 7 (PV-IN CS: day 1: 15.26% ± 2.11%, day 7: 24.09% ± 2.98%; PV-IN reward: day 1: 20.17% ± 3.27%, day 7: 27.47% ± 3.66%; VIP-IN CS: day 1: 11.29% ± 3.23%, day 7: 16.59% ± 2.01%, VIP-IN reward: day 1: 18.65% ± 5.91%, day 7: 26.3% ± 6.04%; Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing observed responses to null distributions, shown in Figure 2F, G.

claim: PN responses to the CS were not different from the null distribution on both days 1 and 7.
source: PN responses to the CS were not different from the null distribution on both days 1 and 7 (day 1: 18.42% ± 1.05%, day 7: 16.41% ± 1.33%; Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PN responses to the reward were significantly higher on day 1 but significantly lower than the null distribution on day 7.
source: in contrast, PN responses to the reward were significantly higher on day 1 but significantly lower than the null distribution on day 7 (day 1: 23.95% ± 2.49%, day 7: 12.12% ± 0.95%; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SOM-INs showed significant responses to the CS and reward only on day 7 following associative learning.
source: Lastly, SOM-INs showed significant responses to the CS and reward only on day 7 following associative learning, while on day 1, they demonstrated no response to the CS and a modest response to the reward (CS: day 1: 5.53% ± 2.7%, day 7: 13.56% ± 3.17%; Reward: day 1: 9% ± 3.66%, day 7: 12.15% ± 3.93%; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The average percent of CS-responsive PV-INs during a trial increased significantly by day 7.
source: When we compared the mean percent of CS-responsive neurons on days 1 and 7, we found that the average percent of CS-responsive PV-INs during a trial increased significantly by day 7 (day 1: 15.26% ± 2.11%, day 7: 24.09% ± 2.98%; Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The percent of CS-responsive VIP-INs did not change between days 1 and 7.
source: while the percent of CS-responsive VIP-INs did not change (day 1: 11.29% ± 3.23%, day 7: 16.59% ± 2.01%; Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PV-INs, as a population, were significantly more reliable in their CS responses than VIP-INs on day 1.
source: We observed that PV-INs, as a population, were significantly more reliable in their CS responses than VIP-INs on day 1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by cumulative distribution analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PV-INs that began as highly reliable maintained their reliability to the CS.
source: We found that PV-INs that began as highly reliable maintained their reliability to the CS (day 1: 29.8% ± 1.51%, day 7: 33.87% ± 4.72%)
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PV-INs that began as Low Reliability became significantly more reliable to the CS.
source: while PV-INs that began as Low Reliability became significantly more reliable (8.47% ± 0.46%, day 7: 18.99% ± 3.76%; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The reliability of both High and Low VIP-INs to CS did not change.
source: In contrast, the reliability of both High and Low VIP-INs did not change (High Reliability: day 1: 26.55% ± 2.62%, day 7: 25.93% ± 3.81%; Low Reliability: day 1: 6.32% ± 0.76%, day 7: 14.24% ± 2.6%; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: 97% of the CS-responsive PV-INs from day 1 still showed responsivity to CS on day 7.
source: Furthermore, 97% of the CS-responsive PV-INs from day 1 still showed responsivity to CS on day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In the absence of reward, PV-INs did not show significant responses to tone.
source: Surprisingly, PV-INs did not show significant tone-responsive cells compared to the chance level on either day 1 or 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: When tone was not paired with reward, PV-INs showed significant responses to tone on day 1 but not day 7.
source: Interestingly, by day 7, PV-INs no longer responded to the tone stimulus (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by nonpaired control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: PV-INs and VIP-INs did not show a significant change in the percent of responsive cells per trial to reward.
source: PV-INs and VIP-INs did not show a significant change in the percent of responsive cells per trial (PV-IN: day 1: 20.17% ± 3.27%, day 7: 27.47% ± 3.66%; VIP-IN: day 1: 18.65% ± 5.91%, day 7: 26.3% ± 6.04%; Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: VIP-INs as a population were significantly more reliable than PV-INs to reward on day 1.
source: When we examined the cumulative distribution of reliabilities for reward responses between the two cell types, VIP-INs as a population were significantly more reliable than PV-INs on day 1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by cumulative distribution analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: High Reliability VIP-INs maintained their reliability to reward.
source: we found the High Reliability VIP-INs maintained their reliability (VIP-IN High Reliability: day 1: 38.79% ± 2.71%, day 7: 35.88% ± 4.32%)
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Low Reliability VIP-INs became significantly more reliable to reward on day 7.
source: and the Low Reliability VIP-INs became significantly more reliable on day 7 (VIP-IN Low Reliability: day 1: 10.25% ± 1.67%, day 7: 24.06% ± 4.87%; Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: Both High and Low Reliability PV-INs maintained their reliability to reward.
source: In contrast, both High and Low Reliability PV-INs maintained their reliability to reward (High Reliability: day 1: 35.59% ± 2.81%, day 7: 41.94% ± 5.7%; Low Reliability: day 1: 10.58% ± 0.74%, day 7: 19.59% ± 3.08%; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: 95% of the VIP-INs from day 1 still showed responsivity to reward on day 7.
source: Furthermore, 95% of the VIP-INs from day 1 still showed responsivity to reward on day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: PNs initially responded to novel reward; however, they habituated to the reward following associative learning.
source: These results indicate that PNs initially responded to novel reward; however, they habituated to the reward following associative learning.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6A, B showing decreased PN reward responses on day 7.

claim: SOM-INs were unresponsive to the CS on day 1 but became more reliably responsive to the CS following associative learning.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that in naive mice, SOM-INs were unresponsive to the CS and modestly responsive to the novel reward; however, following associative learning, SOM-INs became more reliably responsive to both the CS and reward.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C, D showing increased SOM-IN CS responses on day 7.

claim: SOM-INs became more reliably responsive to reward following associative learning.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that in naive mice, SOM-INs were unresponsive to the CS and modestly responsive to the novel reward; however, following associative learning, SOM-INs became more reliably responsive to both the CS and reward.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6E, F showing increased SOM-IN reward responses on day 7.

claim: In each cell type, the majority of the neurons were nonlick neurons on both days 1 and 7.
source: We observed that in each cell type, the majority of the neurons were nonlick neurons on both days 1 and 7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by licking analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All cell types exhibited lower reliability index values for the ITI lick bouts compared to the CS and reward.
source: Lastly, at the population level, we examined the response reliability index of all the active neurons during all ITI lick bouts and compared them to the response reliability index for the CS and reward. On both day 1 (when there was minimal anticipatory licking during the CS) and day 7 (when mice showed anticipatory licking), all cell types exhibited lower reliability index values for the ITI lick bouts compared to the CS and reward, indicating that the increase in task-related responses following water rewards was specific to the reward stimulus, and not licking movements (Figure 7D–J).
evidence: This is supported by reliability analysis shown in Figure 7D–J.

claim: Licking is an innate movement that does not induce plastic changes in adult mice.
source: However, since licking is an innate movement that does not induce plastic changes in adult mice (Chen et al., 2015; Komiyama et al., 2010; Peters et al., 2014), we can reliably attribute changes in neuronal activity over the course of the task to associative learning, rather than motor learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PV-INs in M1 only respond to behaviorally relevant cues such as those that predict reward.
source: This suggests that in M1, PV-INs only respond to behaviorally relevant cues such as those that predict reward.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PV-INs respond to tone when paired with reward but not when tone is presented alone or unpaired.

claim: M1 is unlikely to be a primary site for learning reward predictions.
source: An interesting point to note is that since PV-INs are only responsive to tone when it is paired with reward, and neither PV-INs nor VIP-INs undergo plastic changes in the absence of associative learning, M1 is unlikely to be a primary site for learning reward predictions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PV-INs and VIP-INs do not show changes in the absence of associative learning.

claim: Other brain regions are responsible for learning relevant CS–reward associations while filtering out behaviorally irrelevant stimuli, and these regions subsequently send long-range inputs to M1 to instruct motor responses to the CS and the reward.
source: We hypothesize that other brain regions are responsible for learning relevant CS–reward associations while filtering out behaviorally irrelevant stimuli, and these regions subsequently send long-range inputs to M1 to instruct motor responses to the CS and the reward.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the inference that M1 is not the primary site for learning reward predictions.

claim: During CS–reward conditioning, PV-INs in M1 encode the CS association, and may regulate local circuit activity related to reward anticipation.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that during CS–reward conditioning, PV-INs in M1 encode the CS association, and may regulate local circuit activity related to reward anticipation, whereas VIP-INs act as a context-dependent switch following the reward delivery (Muñoz et al., 2017; Turi et al., 2019) to instruct and disinhibit local PNs to enable learning-induced plastic changes critical for the acquisition of new movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PV-INs become more reliable to CS after learning.

claim: VIP-INs act as a context-dependent switch following the reward delivery to instruct and disinhibit local PNs to enable learning-induced plastic changes critical for the acquisition of new movements.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that during CS–reward conditioning, PV-INs in M1 encode the CS association, and may regulate local circuit activity related to reward anticipation, whereas VIP-INs act as a context-dependent switch following the reward delivery (Muñoz et al., 2017; Turi et al., 2019) to instruct and disinhibit local PNs to enable learning-induced plastic changes critical for the acquisition of new movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VIP-INs become more reliable to reward after learning, combined with citations to prior work on VIP-IN function.
